segments.english: At that time Abimelech and Phichol, the commander of his army, said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do.
segments.literal: and-it-came-to-pass in-the-time the-that and-said Abimelech and-Phichol commander-of his-army to Abraham saying God with-you in-all that you-doing

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of הָיָה, 3rd masculine singular. It is the narrative formula that opens the scene; the English has no word for it.
הַהִוא: the demonstrative with the article, after a noun that has the article.
Wayyiqtol of אָמַר; the subject follows the verb.
King of Gerar, the first sense the pack lists for this name.
שַׂר in the construct state, with the noun that follows.
Infinitive construct with לְ. It introduces the speech; the English marks the speech with quotation marks.
Plural in form, used of the God whom Abraham serves. The pack's 'the (true) God' (3) is not chosen: the speaker does not set this God against other gods.
כֹּל with the relative clause that follows: 'everything that'.
Active participle, masculine singular, in a relative clause: 'you are doing', rendered 'you do'.

phrases.literal: and-it-came-to-pass: the narrative formula, with no English counterpart
to-say: introduces the speech, which the quotation marks render
God with-you; the clause has no verb, and 'is' is the English copula

grammar: The verse opens a scene. The wayyiqtol וַיְהִי (21:22.1) is a narrative formula, and the wayyiqtol וַיֹּאמֶר (21:22.4) carries the story on; its subject follows the verb, as usual in this construction.
אֱלֹהִים עִמְּךָ בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּה עֹשֶׂה is a verbless clause. 'Is' in the English is the copula the Hebrew does not express.
לֵאמֹר (21:22.11) is the infinitive construct that introduces direct speech. Its etnaḥta divides the verse before the speech.
The participle עֹשֶׂה (21:22.17) in the relative clause gives a continuing practice: 'in all that you do'.
segments.note: The copula 'is' is the only word added to the verbless clause. The divine name takes the sense 'God' (4); the note on 21:22.12 gives the reason.

commentary.summary: Radak dates the time to when Isaac was born or weaned, while Abraham was still in Gerar in the land of the Philistines. The English keeps 'that time' and does not fix a date.

Rashi: they (Abimelech and Phichol) said this because they saw that Abraham had come out of the neighbourhood of Sodom in peace, had fought the kings and they fell into his hand, and that his wife had been visited (with a child) for his old age. That is a motive, not a reading of the words.
Radak explains why the verse says 'said' and not 'went to': Abimelech wanted Abraham as an ally after he saw Abraham's success. A reason for the speech, not a reading of its words.
Radak says Phichol's counsel lay behind Abimelech's words. A motive, not a reading of the words.
Onkelos renders the clause as 'the Memra of the LORD is at your side', a targumic rendering of the divine name. The English keeps 'God' for אֱלֹהִים, as the decisions set.

Sforno: 'therefore I fear you, not your might and wealth; so I ask that you swear' (the comment breaks off at the request for the oath). He gives Abimelech's reason for asking an oath; it is a motive, not a reading of the words.

context: Gerar is the town where Abimelech holds court (20:1; 26:1). Its site is not established by the text.

Abimelech's people are called Philistines in 21:32 and 26:1. Most historians date the settlement of Philistines on the coast to the 12th century BCE, long after the patriarchal period. Some read the name here as a later label; others take it as a term the narrator used in his own time. The English does not use the word in this verse.

segments.english: Now swear to me by God here that you will not deal falsely with me, or with my offspring, or with my posterity; as the kindness that I did with you, you shall do with me and with the land in which you have sojourned."
segments.literal: and-now swear to-me by-God here if you-deal-falsely to-me and-to my-offspring and-to my-grandson as-the-kindness which I-did with-you you-will-do with-me and-with the-land which you-sojourned in-it

tokens.note: וְ with עַתָּה: 'now', marking the turn from the past kindness to the request.
Niphal imperative, masculine singular, with the paragogic ה (הִשָּׁבְעָה). Its Niphal sense is 'swear, take an oath'.
The preposition לְ with the first person suffix.
בְּ with the plural divine name, in an oath formula.
The adverb 'here, hither': the oath is taken in the present company.
After a verb of swearing, אִם introduces the oath and makes it negative: 'that you will not ...' (an elided curse: '[may such and such befall me] if ...'). The abridged BDB lists only 'if', sense 1.

Qal yiqtol, 2nd masculine singular of שָׁקַר, 'deal falsely'. Ibn Ezra: it is 'from the light binyan and has no brother', that is, the Qal form occurs nowhere else; elsewhere the root is Piel (the lexicon lists a Pi: 'deal falsely').
נִין: a descendant. Radak takes it as 'son'; see the commentary.
נֶכֶד: Ibn Ezra's 'son of my son'. The lexicon's 'progeny' is wider; see the commentary.
כְּ 'as, like' with חֶסֶד, the kindness that Abraham showed Abimelech.
Qatal 1st common singular of עָשָׂה. 'Do kindness with someone' (עָשָׂה חֶסֶד עִם) is the idiom; the second verb of the comparison, 21:23.15, is the same root.
Yiqtol 2nd masculine singular: the future of the request.
The country in which Abraham sojourned, the sense 'country, territory'.
Qatal 2nd masculine singular of גּוּר: to live as a resident who is not a citizen.
בָּהּ: the feminine suffix refers to אֶרֶץ, 'land'.

phrases.literal: if: after a verb of swearing, אִם is the oath formula, "(may it be so) if": a negative oath, "that ... not"

phrases.english: you will not deal falsely with me
phrases.literal: you-deal-falsely to-me: the negative comes from the oath formula אִם, not from a word of its own
you-will-do with-me; the yiqtol has the force of a request

grammar: The oath opens with the Niphal imperative הִשָּׁבְעָה and the conditional אִם, and the conditional has no apodosis. The curse that would complete it is left unstated, as Ramban explains; the English keeps the clause open.

The verb תִּשְׁקֹר (21:23.7) is a yiqtol in a conditional clause. Ibn Ezra: 'from the light binyan, and it has no brother': it is a Qal, a form found only here; the English reads it as Qal, 'deal falsely'.
Three persons are named after the verb, each with the preposition לְ: 'to me', 'to my offspring', 'to my grandson'. The English repeats 'with' before each.

כַּחֶסֶד אֲשֶׁר־עָשִׂיתִי עִמְּךָ (21:23.11–14) is the first half of a correlative 'as ... so': 'as the kindness that I did with you, you shall do with me'. The second verb, תַּעֲשֶׂה, is a yiqtol with the force of a request.
The etnaḥta on וּלְנֶכְדִּי (21:23.10) divides the verse: the oath and the persons it covers before it, the demand for like kindness after it. The geresh on כַּחֶסֶד (21:23.11) opens the second half.
The last clause (21:23.17–21) adds the land as a second object of the same request. The feminine suffix in בָּהּ (21:23.21) refers to אֶרֶץ.
segments.note: The oath is a conditional with no apodosis: 'if you deal falsely with me' stands by itself, and the English does not complete it. A reading that completes it as 'that you will not deal falsely' is common, but the Hebrew has no negative, so the English does not add one.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra, on תִּשְׁקֹר: «מֵהַבִּנְיָן הַקַּל וְאֵין לוֹ אָח», 'from the light binyan, and it has no brother'. He places the form in the Qal (the light binyan) and says it has no 'brother': there is no other example of this form in Scripture (the lexicon too lists the Qal only here, the rest being Piel). The English reads Qal, 'deal falsely'.
Ibn Ezra, on נכדי: «בֶּן בְּנִי», 'son of my son'. The English gives 'grandson'.
Rashi remarks that the father's compassion for the son extends only as far as the grandson. A remark on the list of persons, not a reading of the words.

Rashi, citing Genesis Rabbah, names the kindness: Abimelech's earlier words to Abraham, 'Look, my land is before you' (see 20:15). The English says 'the kindness that I did with you' and does not name it.

Ramban explains that אִם in an oath is a conditional whose curse is left unstated, with parallels in 1 Samuel 3:14 and Psalm 89:36. The English keeps the clause without its apodosis, as the Hebrew has it.
Radak reads אִם as 'perhaps' (אוּלַי), not as a condition: 'perhaps you will deal falsely with me'. The English keeps 'if'.

Radak: 'therefore I asked you for an oath', for Abimelech knows that after the oath Abraham will not deal falsely, and Abraham's sons and grandsons will see his oath and keep it. A reason for the request, not a reading of the words.
Radak takes נִין as 'son' and נֶכֶד as 'son's son', citing Isaiah 14:22. The English keeps 'offspring' for נִין, which covers descendants more widely.
Radak says the kindness was Abimelech's: he gave his land before Abraham to dwell in as he wished, and honoured him. The Hebrew names no particular kindness, so the English does not state one.

Radak reads עִם הָאָרֶץ as 'with its inhabitants after me': you and your sons after you shall likewise do kindness and good to them, since you found in the land and its people what you wished. The English keeps 'the land'.

Sforno: 'do with me the kindness (of) swearing on behalf of your sons'. He takes the kindness asked to be that Abraham swears for his sons as well as himself. A reason for the request, not a reading of the words.

apparatus: Radak reads אִם as 'perhaps' rather than 'if'. The English keeps 'if'; the commentary records his reading.
context: In the ancient Near East an oath was sworn by invoking a god as witness and as the one who would punish its breaking, and treaties and agreements were commonly sealed by one. Here Abimelech asks that Abraham swear by God.

חֶסֶד is faithful, kind conduct such as people owe one another through kinship, hospitality or agreement. Scholars disagree about whether the word is a technical term of treaties; the English uses 'kindness' only.
גּוּר (21:23.20) describes a resident who lives in a land that is not his own. The text does not say what rights that status brought.

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol; the reply follows at once.
The independent pronoun, emphatic: it sets Abraham's answer against the request.
Niphal yiqtol, 1st common singular. The Niphal of שָׁבַע is the form used of the one who takes the oath.

grammar: The reply has three parts: a wayyiqtol, the name, and a pronoun with a yiqtol. The independent pronoun אָנֹכִי adds emphasis ("I, for my part, will swear"); English can show it only by stress.
אִשָּׁבֵעַ is the Niphal yiqtol of שָׁבַע, the same stem as the imperative in 21:23.
Accents: the pashta on the verb and the zaqef qaton on the name divide the narrative frame from the reply. The silluq on אִשָּׁבֵעַ ends the verse.

commentary.summary: Radak adds 'and you too swear likewise', reading Abraham's answer as a call for a mutual oath. The English does not add it.
Radak notes the vowel of the first letter of the Niphal form. A point of form that the English does not depend on.
Onkelos renders the verb as 'I will confirm' (אֲנָא אֲקַיֵּם), taking it as making a word good. The English keeps 'swear', the sense of the Niphal in the lexicon.
Sforno reads the reply as a contrast: Abraham will do the kindness and swear, but Abimelech did not do kindness to him. A reading of the reply's logic that the words do not state.

segments.english: Abraham rebuked Abimelech concerning the well of the water which the servants of Abimelech seized.
segments.literal: and-rebuked Abraham [object] Abimelech on account-of well-of the-water which seized servants-of Abimelech

tokens.note: Hifil qatal, 3rd masculine singular, of יָכַח: 'reprove, chide'. Rashi reads a reciprocal sense; see the commentary.
The object marker before the name; no English counterpart.
עַל: 'on', with the noun that follows.
אֹדוֹת: a construct noun in a fixed phrase, 'concerning'. The pack lists no senses for it.
בְּאֵר in the construct state: 'well of'.
מַיִם: a plural noun, with the article.
Qatal 3rd common plural of גָּזַל: 'tear away, seize, rob'. The subject is the servants.

phrases.english: which the servants of Abimelech seized

grammar: The verb וְהוֹכִחַ (21:25.1) is a Hifil qatal with a simple וְ, not a wayyiqtol: the clause does not simply carry the story forward and may be read as background ('Abraham had reproved'). The English keeps the plain past; Radak takes it as the next event.
אֹדוֹת (21:25.6) is a noun in a fixed phrase, עַל־אֹדוֹת, 'on account of, concerning'. The pack lists no senses for it.
The relative clause (21:25.9–12) has the servants as subject. The seizure is theirs, and the verb is qatal.
The object marker אֶת has no English counterpart; the English gives the name as the object of 'rebuked' by word order.

commentary.summary: Rashi reads וְהוֹכִחַ as reciprocal: 'they argued with him about this' (נִתְוַכֵּחַ עִמּוֹ). The English keeps Abraham's reproof, the sense of the Hifil form.

Radak places the well inside the border of Beersheba, which Abraham had dug, and says the parties went to Gerar to see whether it lay on Beersheba's border or on Philistine land. The Hebrew does not give the location, so the English does not state it.
Sforno takes the rebuke more widely: against Abimelech's failure to stop robbery in his land, and against the wicked in his household. The English gives the rebuke about the well only.

context: In dry country a dug well was valuable property, and rights over wells were a common cause of dispute (compare 26:15–22). The dispute in this verse is over a well and the water in it. The text does not say where the well lay.

segments.english: Abimelech said, "I did not know who did this thing. And you also did not tell me, and I also did not hear until today."
segments.literal: and-said Abimelech not I-knew who did [object] the-thing this and-also you not you-told to-me and-also I not heard except the-today

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of אָמַר; the subject follows the verb.
The negation of the qatal that follows.
Qatal 1st common singular of יָדַע; with the preceding לֹא, 'I did not know'.
Interrogative in an indirect question inside the speech.
Qatal 3rd masculine singular of עָשָׂה.
The object marker before the noun phrase.
דָּבָר in the sense 'matter, affair'.
The demonstrative in apposition to the noun.
וְגַם: the first of two parallel clauses.
The negation of the qatal that follows.
Hifil qatal 2nd masculine singular of נָגַד: 'declare, tell'.
The preposition לְ with the first person suffix.
וְגַם: the second clause of the parallel.
The negation of the qatal that follows.
Qatal 1st common singular of שָׁמַע.
בִּלְתִּי: 'not, except'. Here the phrase is 'except today', rendered 'until today'.
הַיּוֹם: the noun 'day' with the article, in the adverbial phrase 'today'.

phrases.english: And you also did not tell me
and I also did not hear until today
phrases.literal: and-also I not heard except today

grammar: לֹא יָדַעְתִּי (21:26.3–4) is a qatal with the negative: 'I did not know'. The negative and the verb are separate tokens.
מִי עָשָׂה אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה (21:26.5–9) is an indirect question inside the speech: 'who did this thing'.
The two clauses joined by וְגַם (21:26.10–18) form a parallel pair: 'you did not tell me' and 'I did not hear'. The English keeps the parallel with 'also'.
בִּלְתִּי הַיּוֹם (21:26.19–20) is literally 'except today'. The English 'until today' gives the sense the phrase has in this clause.
הִגַּדְתָּ (21:26.13) is a Hifil qatal, 2nd masculine singular: 'you told'. The thing told is not named, so the English leaves it unstated.

commentary.summary: Sforno: even now that Abraham has told him the robbery was done by his servants, Abimelech cannot say which of them did it, since none is suspect to him. The English keeps 'I did not know who did this thing'.
Sforno explains why Abimelech as king would have acted had he known: the king would act on a cry from the robbed or on public report. A reason, not a reading of the words.
Radak says that since Abraham has now told him, Abimelech bears no guilt. A conclusion drawn from the speech, which the English does not state.

apparatus: בִּלְתִּי הַיּוֹם is literally 'except today'. The English renders it 'until today', the sense of the phrase in this clause.

segments.english: Abraham took flocks and cattle and gave to Abimelech, and they both made a covenant.
segments.literal: and-took Abraham flocks and-cattle and-gave to-Abimelech and-cut they-both a-covenant

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of לָקַח, 3rd masculine singular. The things taken are the flocks and cattle.
צֹאן: small livestock, sheep and goats. The pack lists no senses.
בָּקָר: cattle, herd. The pack lists no senses.
Wayyiqtol of נָתַן. The verb has no stated object: the animals are the things given.
Wayyiqtol 3rd masculine plural of כָּרַת. The idiom is 'cut a covenant'; the English is 'make a covenant'.
The dual construct with the pronominal suffix: 'both of them'.
בְּרִית between men: an agreement between Abraham and Abimelech.

grammar: Three wayyiqtols carry the verse: took, gave, and made a covenant. The subject of the last is 'they', the two men together.
נָתַן (21:27.5) has no stated object. The English gives 'gave to Abimelech' without an object, as the Hebrew does; the reader supplies the flocks and cattle from the clause before.
וַיִּכְרְתוּ בְּרִית (21:27.7–9) is 'they cut a covenant'. The English 'made' is the idiom; the literal line keeps 'cut'.
שְׁנֵיהֶם (21:27.8) is 'both of them': it stresses that both parties made the covenant.
segments.note: The object of נָתַן is not stated, so the English leaves it unstated.

commentary.summary: Radak explains that the gift was for confirming the covenant, and that the covenant was made for the two parties and their sons. A reason, not a reading of the words.

context: The verse reports a gift of livestock and a covenant; the oath was asked and given in 21:23–24. 'Cut a covenant' is the Hebrew idiom; it is often linked with the ancient Near Eastern practice of cutting up animals in sealing a treaty (compare 15:9–10, 17), but this verse describes no such rite, and the English keeps to the words.

segments.english: Abraham set seven ewe-lambs of the flock by themselves.
segments.literal: and-set Abraham [object] seven ewe-lambs of-the-flock by-themselves

tokens.note: Hifil wayyiqtol of נָצַב: 'station, set'. Its object is the seven ewe-lambs.
The object marker before the noun phrase; no English counterpart.
כִּבְשׂוֹת: the construct plural of כִּבְשָׂה, 'ewe-lamb'.
הַצֹּאן: the second term of the construct chain.
לְבַדְּהֶן in the text: לְ with בַּד ('separation, alone') and the feminine plural suffix -hen, 'by themselves' (of the ewe-lambs).

grammar: The Hifil of נָצַב means 'station, set'. Its object here is the seven ewe-lambs, which Abraham sets apart.
כִּבְשֹׂת הַצֹּאן (21:28.5–6) is a construct chain: 'ewe-lambs of the flock'.
לְבַדְּהֶן (21:28.7) has the feminine plural suffix -hen, which refers back to the ewe-lambs; 21:29 has the form לְבַדָּנָה.
Wordplay: שֶׁבַע, 'seven', shares its root with the verb שָׁבַע, 'swear' (21:23). The text makes the link explicit at 21:31.

commentary.summary: Radak: from the sheep and cattle Abraham had given, he took seven ewe-lambs and set them apart by themselves; he took seven because the word for the number and the word for oath are one, and it would be a witness (the comment breaks off). The English keeps the separation of the seven.

Radak: the seven ewe-lambs stand together with the oath as a witness for later generations, since the covenant was made with the seven ewe-lambs and the oath; therefore he named the place Beersheba. The name is explained in 21:31, not here.

segments.english: Abimelech said to Abraham, "What are these, these seven ewe-lambs that you have set by themselves?"
segments.literal: and-said Abimelech to Abraham what these seven ewe-lambs these which you-set by-themselves

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of אָמַר.
The interrogative מָה: 'what'.
הֵנָּה: the feminine plural pronoun, agreeing with the ewe-lambs. Ibn Ezra notes the feminine form.
The demonstrative after the noun. The noun has no article, so the demonstrative is attributive: 'these', not 'the ... these'.
Hifil qatal, 2nd masculine singular: 'you set'.
לְבַדָּנָה: a feminine form with the suffix נָה; Ibn Ezra's comment is in the commentary.

phrases.literal: seven ewe-lambs the-these; the demonstrative is repeated after הֵנָּה

phrases.english: that you have set by themselves

grammar: מָה הֵנָּה (21:29.5–6) is a verbless question: 'what (are) these?'. The English supplies the copula 'are'. The answer is given by the apposition: 'these seven ewe-lambs'.
הָאֵלֶּה (21:29.9) repeats the demonstrative after the noun and carries the article though the noun שֶׁבַע כְּבָשֹׂת has none; the English repeats 'these'.
אֲשֶׁר הִצַּבְתָּ (21:29.10–11) is a relative clause with a Hifil qatal, 2nd masculine singular. The addressee is Abraham.
הֵנָּה and לְבַדָּנָה are feminine plural forms, agreeing with the ewe-lambs (שֶׁבַע כְּבָשֹׂת). English has no feminine; 'these' and 'by themselves' are plural.
The question ends with the silluq on לְבַדָּנָה (21:29.12). The zaqef qaton on הָאֵלֶּה (21:29.9) divides the question from the relative clause.
segments.note: Ibn Ezra's reading of לְבַדָּנָה is in the commentary and the apparatus; the English keeps the plural.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra, on מָה הֵנָּה: «לְשׁוֹן נְקֵבוֹת», 'the language of females': הֵנָּה is the feminine plural pronoun, said of the ewe-lambs. English cannot show the gender; 'these' is plural.

Ibn Ezra, on לְבַדָּנָה: «עִם ה״א וְהִיא לְבַדָּהּ», 'with a heh; and it is lebadah'. He takes the form as the feminine of 'by himself', 'alone' (a form ending in heh), the counterpart of לְבַדָּהּ, 'by herself'; he does not say it is plural. The English 'by themselves' gives the sense for the seven ewe-lambs; the suffix -nah is a feminine plural suffix by the pack's parse, so the English keeps the plural, and records his equation with the singular form.

apparatus: Ibn Ezra equates לְבַדָּנָה with לְבַדָּהּ ('alone', feminine singular, 'by herself'). The English keeps the plural 'by themselves' for the seven ewe-lambs, the sense the feminine plural suffix -nah gives in the pack's parse.
